facts.title: Decoding the RFC 5424 priority value
facts.fact: An RFC 5424 message starts with a priority value in angle brackets, computed as facility multiplied by eight plus severity. Facility names the subsystem that produced the message, for example 4 for auth and 16 for local0, while severity runs from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug). A receiver must decode the integer before it can route, filter, or compare the message with events from other facilities.
details: PRI 38 decodes to facility 4 (auth) and severity 6 (informational), because 4 x 8 + 6 = 38.
PRI 134 decodes to facility 16 (local0) and severity 6 (informational), because 16 x 8 + 6 = 134.
A relay may re-emit a message under its own facility, so the PRI seen at the collector is not always the PRI the originator wrote.
pitfalls: Ranking messages by the numeric PRI: local1.debug (135) is larger than kern.emerg (0) even though it is far less urgent.
Treating facility as a severity signal; facility only says which subsystem spoke.

logs.context: RFC 5424 line from an SSH daemon
logs.text: <38>1 2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z bastion-01 sshd 2411 ID47 - Accepted publickey for jdoe from 192.0.2.44 port 51234 ssh2
logs.reading: The leading <38> is facility 4 (auth) and severity 6 (informational). The event is therefore an ordinary auth-subsystem informational record, not an emergency, even though 38 is numerically larger than many low-severity PRI values.

mcqs.question: A syslog record begins with <134>. Which facility and severity does the value encode?
options: local0.info
auth.info
local0.debug
kern.notice
mcqs.rationale: 134 = 16 x 8 + 6, so facility 16 (local0) and severity 6 (informational). auth is facility 4 and would give values from 32 to 39.

facts.title: The RFC 5424 header fields and NILVALUE
facts.fact: After the priority and version, RFC 5424 defines TIMESTAMP, HOSTNAME, APP-NAME, PROCID, MSGID, STRUCTURED-DATA and then an optional free-form MSG. Any header field that has no value is written as a single hyphen, called NILVALUE. The fields are space-delimited, so a parser must respect the hyphen convention instead of assuming every position is populated.
details: TIMESTAMP is an RFC 3339 timestamp with an explicit offset or Z, and may carry up to six fractional-second digits.
HOSTNAME, APP-NAME, PROCID and MSGID are originator-supplied strings; none of them is authenticated by the protocol.
MSGID is meant to identify the type of message, for example a vendor event code, and is not the same thing as a sequence number.
pitfalls: Assuming PROCID is always a numeric process ID; the field may be NILVALUE or a vendor string.
Trusting HOSTNAME as an authenticated identity. Any sender can claim any hostname.

logs.context: Header field walk-through of one syslog record
logs.text: <38>1 2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z bastion-01 sshd 2411 ID47 - Accepted publickey for jdoe from 192.0.2.44 port 51234 ssh2
logs.reading: VERSION is 1, TIMESTAMP is 2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z, HOSTNAME is bastion-01, APP-NAME is sshd, PROCID is 2411, MSGID is ID47, STRUCTURED-DATA is the NILVALUE hyphen, and MSG is the remainder starting with 'Accepted publickey'.

mcqs.question: Which RFC 5424 header field names the application or process that generated the message?
options: APP-NAME
MSGID
PROCID
HOSTNAME
mcqs.rationale: APP-NAME carries the application name such as sshd or nginx. MSGID identifies the message type, PROCID is a process identifier, and HOSTNAME is the originator's claimed host name.

facts.title: Structured data is not a replacement for parsing MSG
facts.fact: RFC 5424 structured data is a sequence of bracketed SD-ELEMENTs, each with an SD-ID and optional space-separated name=value parameters. A private SD-ID conventionally ends in an @ followed by an enterprise number, which keeps vendor fields from colliding. Parameters are quoted, and the characters double quote, backslash and closing bracket must be escaped inside a value.
details: A record may carry several SD-ELEMENTs; each starts with a fresh bracketed SD-ID.
Structured data is optional, and many real deployments still emit the NILVALUE hyphen.
Values remain strings; the protocol does not define types or units for them.
pitfalls: Assuming structured data makes MSG unnecessary. Only fields the sender chose to declare appear there.
Writing a naive splitter on spaces or quotes; escaped characters and the closing bracket rule break simple parsers.

logs.context: RFC 5424 record with a vendor structured-data element
logs.text: <165>1 2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z app-01 cron 2211 ID47 [exampleSDID@32473 iut="3" eventSource="Application" eventID="1011"] job=nightly-backup status=started
logs.reading: PRI 165 is local4.notice. The sender declares three parameters in a private enterprise SD-ELEMENT, then repeats similar context in free-form MSG. A parser should take the declared parameters as authoritative and avoid re-parsing the MSG for the same values.

misconceptions.claim: Once a syslog sender emits structured data, the message body no longer needs to be parsed.
misconceptions.correction: Structured data only contains parameters the sender explicitly declared. The MSG field remains free-form and often carries the only copy of the event detail, so pipelines still need a message parser or a documented format contract.

facts.title: Why RFC 3164 timestamps need external context
facts.fact: The older BSD syslog format, documented in RFC 3164, writes a timestamp as 'Mmm dd hh:mm:ss' with no year and no time zone. A collector must infer the year from its own clock and assume a local time zone that is rarely stated in the message. Around a year boundary or after a time-zone change, that inference can place events in the wrong day or the wrong order.
details: Single-digit days are commonly space-padded, so 'Nov  8' and 'Nov 18' differ by one character in a fixed-width position.
RFC 3164 has no structured-data field, so everything after the hostname is free-form text.
RFC 5424 was designed to remove these ambiguities, but many appliances still default to the older format.
pitfalls: Sorting mixed RFC 3164 and RFC 5424 streams by their raw timestamp strings; the formats are not lexicographically comparable.
Letting each collector infer the year independently, which produces different dates for the same message after a replay.

logs.context: BSD-format syslog line from an SSH daemon
logs.text: <38>Nov 18 08:14:22 bastion-01 sshd[2411]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.77 port 51001 ssh2
logs.reading: The line records no year and no offset. A collector in UTC would store 2026-11-18T08:14:22Z only if its own clock says 2026 and its configured zone is UTC; the same bytes replayed in a different zone become a different instant.

mcqs.question: Why can an RFC 3164 log line be assigned the wrong date around New Year?
options: The timestamp omits the year, so the collector must infer it
The timestamp uses a 64-bit nanosecond counter
The hostname field contains the date
The priority value changes at midnight
mcqs.rationale: RFC 3164 timestamps contain month, day and time but no year or zone. Collectors infer both, and the inference can be wrong when clocks roll over or streams are replayed.

misconceptions.claim: RFC 3164 timestamps include the year and time zone, so they are directly sortable.
misconceptions.correction: They include neither. The format is 'Mmm dd hh:mm:ss'; year and zone come from collector configuration or inference, which is exactly the ambiguity RFC 5424 set out to fix.

facts.title: JSON logs and the Elastic Common Schema
facts.fact: JSON log lines preserve nesting and types that plain text loses, but they do not by themselves agree on field names. The Elastic Common Schema gives shared names to common concepts, for example event.category, event.outcome, source.ip, user.name and host.name, so one query can span products. Adopting a schema is a mapping project, not a property of JSON.
details: event.category is an array, for example authentication or process, and event.type describes start, end or change.
Nested objects such as source.ip avoid ambiguous flat names like src, sip or client_addr.
A schema reduces guesswork but still needs a documented mapping per log source and a version pin.
pitfalls: Assuming every JSON log uses ECS; @timestamp, time, ts and timestamp can all appear in one estate.
Flattening nested objects without recording the original path, which makes later re-mapping impossible.

logs.context: ECS-shaped authentication event
logs.text: {"@timestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z","event":{"category":["authentication"],"outcome":"failure","dataset":"linux.auth"},"host":{"name":"bastion-01"},"user":{"name":"jdoe"},"source":{"ip":"203.0.113.77"},"message":"Failed password for jdoe"}
logs.reading: The fields are typed and nested: source.ip is a single value, event.category is an array, and the timestamp is explicitly UTC. A query can group by source.ip without knowing which product produced the line, provided every source was mapped to the same schema version.

mcqs.question: Which ECS field holds the source IP address of a network event?
options: source.ip
client.ip
network.src
host.ip
mcqs.rationale: ECS uses source.ip for the initiator and destination.ip for the target. host.ip describes addresses assigned to the monitored host, not the remote peer.

facts.title: CEF and LEEF: pipe headers with vendor-defined extensions
facts.fact: CEF and LEEF are line-oriented formats built for security event collectors. CEF starts with a fixed pipe-delimited header that ends in a severity value, then an extension of key=value pairs; LEEF uses a similar header and a delimiter, commonly a caret in version 1.0, before its key=value pairs. The headers are standardized, but the extension keys are only partly standardized, so a parser needs the vendor's dictionary.
details: A CEF header carries version, device vendor, device product, device version, signature ID, name and severity, in that order.
Escaping matters: a literal pipe or equals sign inside a value is normally protected with a backslash.
Many products reuse generic slots such as cs1 with a companion cs1Label, which means the meaning lives in the label, not the key.
pitfalls: Assuming a key such as suser or outcome means the same thing in every product; verify the vendor extension dictionary.
Splitting on every pipe without honouring escapes, which truncates values that contain the delimiter.

logs.context: CEF authentication failure
logs.text: CEF:0|Example Corp|SSO Gateway|2.4.1|AUTH-1102|Failed login|5|src=203.0.113.77 suser=jdoe outcome=failure cs1Label=TenantId cs1=tenant-0042
logs.reading: The header identifies vendor, product, version, signature AUTH-1102, human name and severity 5. The extension supplies source address, subject user, outcome and a vendor-labelled tenant slot. The numeric severity is device-defined; it is not the same scale as syslog severity.

logs.context: LEEF 1.0 authentication event
logs.text: LEEF:1.0|Example Corp|SSO Gateway|2.4.1|AUTH-1102|src=203.0.113.77^usrName=jdoe^cat=Authentication
logs.reading: The caret separates extension pairs. usrName is an IBM QRadar-style key rather than the CEF suser key, which shows why a normalizer must map per format instead of assuming one shared dictionary.

mcqs.question: In a CEF record, where do product-specific fields such as a tenant identifier appear?
options: In the extension after the final header pipe
Inside the device product name
In the severity field
Before the CEF:0 prefix
mcqs.rationale: The CEF header ends with severity, and everything after the next pipe is the extension of key=value pairs. Vendor-specific values are usually placed in labelled generic slots such as cs1 with cs1Label.

misconceptions.claim: CEF and LEEF are interchangeable standards with one fixed field dictionary.
misconceptions.correction: Their headers are similar but not identical, and their extension vocabularies differ and are partly vendor-defined. A CEF suser and a LEEF usrName may describe the same concept, but a parser must map each format explicitly.

facts.title: The Windows Event Log XML envelope
facts.fact: A rendered Windows event has a System section owned by the logging service and an EventData or UserData section owned by the provider. System carries Provider Name, EventID, Level, Task, Opcode, Keywords, TimeCreated SystemTime, EventRecordID, Channel and Computer. EventData is a list of Data elements whose Name attributes define the payload, and their order is not a stable contract.
details: TimeCreated SystemTime is written in UTC with a Z suffix, independent of the machine's display time zone.
EventRecordID is a per-channel sequence number that helps prove ordering and detect gaps or cleared logs.
The same EventID can mean different things under different Provider and Channel combinations.
pitfalls: Reading EventData by position instead of by the Data Name attribute; providers can add or reorder fields between versions.
Assuming EventID alone is globally meaningful; always qualify it with Provider and Channel.

logs.context: Rendered Security channel event, fields abridged
logs.text:
<Event xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event">
  <System>
    <Provider Name="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing"/>
    <EventID>4625</EventID>
    <Level>0</Level>
    <TimeCreated SystemTime="2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z"/>
    <EventRecordID>884213</EventRecordID>
    <Channel>Security</Channel>
    <Computer>ws-014.example.internal</Computer>
  </System>
  <EventData>
    <Data Name="TargetUserName">jdoe</Data>
    <Data Name="LogonType">3</Data>
    <Data Name="IpAddress">203.0.113.77</Data>
    <Data Name="Status">0xc000006d</Data>
    <Data Name="SubStatus">0xc000006a</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>
logs.reading: The provider plus EventID 4625 identifies a failed logon. LogonType 3 says the attempt arrived over the network, and SubStatus 0xc000006a means the password was wrong for an existing account. The SystemTime is UTC, while the computer's local display might show a different hour.

mcqs.question: In Windows event XML, where does the provider-specific payload normally appear?
options: In EventData Data elements identified by Name
In the EventRecordID element
In the Provider Name attribute only
In the Channel element
mcqs.rationale: EventData holds Data elements whose Name attributes identify the fields. UserData is the alternative shape for some providers. EventRecordID and Channel are System metadata, not the payload.

facts.title: Windows channels, audit policy and event forwarding
facts.fact: Windows Event Log organises records into channels. Security, System and Application are the classic channels, while providers such as Sysmon write to their own operational channels. What appears in Security is decided by audit policy, so a missing event can mean the action did not happen or that the subcategory was never enabled. Windows Event Forwarding can ship selected channels to a collector, where they are stored in the ForwardedEvents log.

references.title: 4688(S): A new process has been created

details: Advanced audit policy is configured per subcategory, for example Process Creation or Logon.
A source-initiated WEF subscription lets many hosts push to one collector without inbound connections to each host.
Forwarded records retain the original Computer and Provider values and add forwarding metadata.
pitfalls: Concluding that no 4688 events means no process ran; process creation auditing may simply be off.
Assuming the Security channel is complete because the service is running.

logs.context: Collector view of forwarded Security events
logs.text:
TimeCreated            ProviderName                            Id    LogName          Computer
18/11/2026 08:14:22    Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing     4625  ForwardedEvents  ws-014.example.internal
18/11/2026 08:14:25    Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing     4624  ForwardedEvents  ws-014.example.internal
logs.reading: The records were read from the ForwardedEvents log, while Computer still names the origin host. A query that reads only the Security log on the collector would miss these copies; use ForwardedEvents or the normalized original channel in the query.

misconceptions.claim: If the Security log does not show an event, the activity did not occur.
misconceptions.correction: The Security channel only contains what audit policy recorded. Process creation, for example, requires the relevant audit subcategory to be enabled; without it the activity can occur with no 4688 record at all.

facts.title: Linux audit events are multi-record and carry auid
facts.fact: The Linux audit subsystem writes a kernel event as several records that share a msg=audit(timestamp:serial) identifier. Typical types are SYSCALL, EXECVE, PATH, CWD and PROCTITLE, while the USER_* records report user-space authentication and command activity, and tools such as ausearch reassemble records by serial. The auid field is the audit UID, or loginuid, captured at login; it normally survives su and sudo, while uid and euid describe the process's current credentials.

references.title: auditd(8) - Linux system audit logging daemon

details: auid is set from the login session and is intended to answer who originally logged in, even after privilege change.
The value 4294967295 (0xFFFFFFFF) means the loginuid was never set, which is common for daemons and containers.
User-space records such as USER_AUTH and USER_CMD can carry their own serials; the session ID and timestamp link them to the same action.
EXECVE arguments may be hex-encoded when they contain spaces or special characters, so a reading tool is safer than string splitting.
The key field echoes the -k label from the rule that matched, which is often more useful than the syscall number.
pitfalls: Reading uid=0 as the human operator while auid holds a different, non-root login identity.
Interpreting auid 4294967295 as a user ID; it is the unset sentinel.

logs.context: sudo command recorded by auditd, records abridged
logs.text:
type=USER_AUTH msg=audit(1794989662.631:4412): pid=2211 uid=0 auid=1000 ses=3 msg='op=PAM:authentication grantors=pam_unix acct="jdoe" exe="/usr/bin/sudo" terminal=/dev/pts/0 res=success'
type=USER_CMD msg=audit(1794989662.631:4413): pid=2211 uid=0 auid=1000 ses=3 msg='cwd="/home/jdoe" cmd=73797374656D63746C2072657374617274206E67696E78 exe="/usr/bin/sudo" terminal=/dev/pts/0 res=success'
logs.reading: uid=0 shows the command ran with root credentials, but auid=1000 preserves the login identity jdoe and ses=3 ties both records to one session. The cmd value is hex and decodes to 'systemctl restart nginx', the argument passed to sudo rather than the wrapper itself.

mcqs.question: In an auditd record, what does the auid field represent?
options: The login UID of the session, normally preserved across privilege changes
The effective UID of the running process
The filesystem UID used for access checks
The audit rule key that matched
mcqs.rationale: auid is the audit UID, also called loginuid, captured from the login session. euid and uid describe current process credentials, and the rule key appears in the key field.

facts.title: Writing audit rules that survive tampering
facts.fact: audit rules attach watches to paths or filters to syscalls and tag matches with a key. A file watch uses -w with a permission filter such as -p wa for write and attribute change, while a syscall rule uses -a always,exit with -F filters and optionally -S to select the syscall. Setting -e 2 makes the configuration immutable until reboot, so an intruder cannot quietly add exclusions or disable auditing.

references.title: auditctl(8) - control the behavior of the audit daemon

details: Rules are loaded in order and watches can overlap; exclude filters are evaluated before ordinary rules and can suppress the events a later rule was meant to catch.
A path watch is attached to the inode present when the rule loads, so replacing the file with a new inode can leave the watch on the old file.
High-volume syscall rules, especially execve across a busy fleet, need sizing and testing before production.
pitfalls: Using -p w alone when owner or mode changes also matter; -p wa covers write and attribute changes.
Assuming -e 2 can be undone without a reboot; it is designed to prevent exactly that.

configs.snippet:
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=4294967295 -k exec
-e 2
configs.purpose: Watch identity and sudoers files, log interactive execve calls, then lock the ruleset until reboot.

logs.context: auditd configuration change record
logs.text: type=CONFIG_CHANGE msg=audit(1794989662.631:99): op=set audit_enabled=2 old=1 auid=4294967295 ses=4294967295 res=1
logs.reading: This record shows the audit subsystem being switched from enabled (1) to immutable (2). After this point, rule changes are refused until reboot, which is why the change should be planned and monitored rather than treated as routine.

facts.title: Reading the web server combined access log
facts.fact: The combined access log appends referer and user agent to the common log format. Its fields are client address, remote identity, authenticated user, request time, request line, status code, response bytes, referer and user agent. Status tells you how the server answered, while bytes tells you how large the response body was, which is often more useful for judging whether an attack returned data.
details: A dash means the field was unavailable, not zero; bytes may be '-' for a 304 or a streamed response.
The client address can be a proxy or load balancer unless the deployment records a trusted forwarding header.
User agent and referer are client-controlled strings and are trivially spoofed.
pitfalls: Treating a 200 response as proof that an injection succeeded; many applications return 200 with a generic error page.
Ignoring response size, which can separate a normal page from a dump of many records.

logs.context: Combined access log, normal request and scanner probe
logs.text:
192.0.2.80 - - [18/Nov/2026:08:14:22 +0000] "GET /product?id=42 HTTP/1.1" 200 8421 "https://example.internal/catalog" "Mozilla/5.0"
198.51.100.10 - - [18/Nov/2026:08:15:01 +0000] "GET /.git/config HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nuclei - Open-source project)"
logs.reading: The first line is an ordinary catalogue request with a normal 8 KB body. The second is a probe for a version-control file, answered with 404 and a small error page. Neither line alone proves intent, but the path and disclosed scanner user agent are consistent with authorised enumeration rather than exploitation.

mcqs.question: In the common or combined access log format, what does the number after the status code represent?
options: The number of bytes in the response body
The request duration in milliseconds
The number of requests from that client
The HTTP protocol version
mcqs.rationale: The field is the response size in bytes, or a dash when the server did not record one. Duration is not part of the standard format and is usually added as an extra field or in a separate log.

facts.title: What firewall, proxy and DNS logs can each prove
facts.fact: Firewall, proxy and DNS telemetry answer different questions and none of them sees inside an encrypted session. A firewall record shows that a flow was permitted or denied for a five-tuple, a proxy record shows request metadata and often the authenticated user, and a DNS record shows which name a client queried. Correlating the three narrows activity, but each layer leaves a different blind spot.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: A firewall allow entry does not show whether the connection succeeded or what was transferred.
A proxy can log full URLs for plain HTTP, but for HTTPS it typically records only host, SNI, certificate metadata and byte counts.
DNS over HTTPS to an external resolver can bypass local DNS logging entirely.
pitfalls: Claiming data was exfiltrated from a DNS query alone; the query shows resolution, not payload delivery.
Assuming proxy logs cover all egress traffic when applications can connect directly to the internet.

logs.context: Firewall, DNS and proxy views of one client
logs.reading: The firewall line shows one blocked flow to 203.0.113.90, the resolver shows a name lookup, and the proxy shows an allowed CONNECT to a different address. The three records describe related but distinct actions: a blocked attempt, a resolution, and a permitted tunnel whose content is not visible.

mcqs.question: A DNS resolver log shows a query for updates.example.net, but no record of the HTTPS upload that followed. What does this illustrate?
options: DNS telemetry shows name resolution, not the content or size of the later transfer
The upload definitely did not happen
Resolver logs contain full HTTP request bodies
TLS encrypts the DNS query itself
mcqs.rationale: DNS logs record the query and response metadata. They do not show whether a connection followed, how many bytes were sent, or what the payload contained; those require proxy, flow or endpoint telemetry.

misconceptions.claim: A firewall allow entry proves that data left the network.
misconceptions.correction: It proves a flow was permitted, not that the handshake completed, that the application sent anything, or what the bytes contained. Confirming transfer needs proxy byte counts, endpoint telemetry or server-side evidence.

facts.title: CloudTrail records and the management versus data event split
facts.fact: CloudTrail writes JSON records with eventTime, eventSource, eventName, awsRegion, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, userIdentity and optional requestParameters, responseElements and errorCode. Management events cover control-plane actions such as creating a user or changing a bucket policy; data events cover object-level actions such as GetObject and are not collected by default. A trail that only records management events will not show reads of individual objects.

references.title: CloudTrail record contents for management, data, and network activity events
Logging Amazon S3 API calls using AWS CloudTrail

details: userIdentity.type distinguishes IAMUser, AssumedRole, Root and AWS service principals, and the ARN identifies the exact principal.
sourceIPAddress can be an AWS service address when the call was made on the account's behalf, so it is not always the human's address.
Delivery is asynchronous; records commonly appear minutes after the API call, so a live alert cannot rely on CloudTrail alone.
pitfalls: Assuming every S3 object read is logged; object-level data events must be enabled and add cost.
Treating a missing record as proof the API was never called, when the event type may simply not be selected.

logs.context: S3 data event from a scheduled backup role
logs.text: {"eventTime":"2026-11-18T08:14:22Z","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com","eventName":"GetObject","awsRegion":"eu-west-1","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.50","userAgent":"aws-cli/2.15.0","userIdentity":{"type":"AssumedRole","arn":"arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/backup-runner/backup-20261118"},"requestParameters":{"bucketName":"example-backups","key":"db/2026/11/18/full.tar.gz"}}
logs.reading: The identity is an assumed role named backup-runner with a session name containing the date, the object key matches the nightly full-backup prefix, and the user agent is the AWS CLI. This is consistent with the documented backup job rather than interactive access.

mcqs.question: Which CloudTrail event category is normally off by default and must be enabled per trail?
options: Data events such as S3 GetObject
Management events such as CreateUser
Sign-in events
Trail status events
mcqs.rationale: Management events are recorded by default. Data events, which include object-level S3 and Lambda invoke activity, have to be enabled and are billed separately because of their volume.

facts.title: Kubernetes audit levels and what they retain
facts.fact: Kubernetes API server audit events record who called which API, from where, with what result. The audit policy assigns a level per request: None records nothing, Metadata records request metadata but not bodies, Request records the body without the response, and RequestResponse records both. Events also carry a stage such as RequestReceived or ResponseComplete, so the same request can produce more than one record.

references.title: Kubernetes API server audit configuration v1

details: objectRef identifies the resource, namespace, name and subresource, which is how exec into a pod appears as a subresource action.
user.username often starts with system: for controllers and system:serviceaccount: for workload identities.
A policy can omit entire namespaces or reduce noisy read-only requests to Metadata, so absence of a body does not imply a failed call.
pitfalls: Assuming RequestResponse is the default; many clusters ship a policy that logs only metadata for high-volume reads.
Confusing the audit log with application logs, which live in containers and are not part of the API server record.

logs.context: Kubernetes audit event for a secret read
logs.text: {"kind":"Event","apiVersion":"audit.k8s.io/v1","level":"RequestResponse","stage":"ResponseComplete","requestURI":"/api/v1/namespaces/payments/secrets/db-creds","verb":"get","user":{"username":"system:serviceaccount:reporting:etl-runner","groups":["system:serviceaccounts","system:authenticated"]},"sourceIPs":["10.20.30.77"],"objectRef":{"resource":"secrets","namespace":"payments","name":"db-creds","apiVersion":"v1"},"responseStatus":{"code":200},"requestReceivedTimestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z","stageTimestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.640Z"}
logs.reading: A workload identity in the reporting namespace read a secret in the payments namespace and received HTTP 200. That crosses a namespace boundary between a reporting job and payment credentials, which is exactly the kind of access to verify against RBAC and the job's stated purpose.

mcqs.question: Which Kubernetes audit level records both the request body and the response body?
options: RequestResponse
Request
Metadata
None
mcqs.rationale: RequestResponse captures both bodies. Request captures only the request body, Metadata captures neither, and None suppresses the event entirely.

facts.title: What endpoint telemetry adds beyond process names
facts.fact: Endpoint detection and response sensors record process creation with the full command line, parent process, image path and often image hash, plus network connections, file writes, registry changes and loaded modules. That context lets an analyst reconstruct a process tree instead of matching a filename. Sysmon provides a comparable subset on Windows through its own event IDs, with event 1 for process creation and event 3 for network connection.

references.title: 4688(S): A new process has been created

details: A process tree with parent-child relationships is stronger evidence than a lone process name, which is easy to reuse.
Image hashes distinguish a legitimate signed binary from a renamed copy with the same filename.
Sensor health matters: a host that stopped reporting has a coverage gap, not a clean bill of health.
pitfalls: Treating a familiar filename such as powershell.exe as benign without checking path, signature and parent.
Ignoring parent PID reuse; verify parent start time rather than trusting the PID alone.

logs.context: Sysmon process creation event, fields abridged
logs.text:
UtcTime: 2026-11-18 08:14:22.631
EventID: 1
Computer: ws-014.example.internal
User: EXAMPLE\jdoe
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoProfile -EncodedCommand <base64 omitted>
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
ParentCommandLine: "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE" /n report.docx
logs.reading: The command line is encoded, but the parent is WINWORD.EXE opening a document, which is not a normal parent for PowerShell. That parent-child pair, not the string powershell.exe by itself, is the high-value observation; the next step is to decode the command and check for a network connection.

mcqs.question: Sysmon event ID 1 records which activity?
options: Process creation
Network connection
DNS query
File creation
mcqs.rationale: Event 1 is Process Create, event 3 is Network Connect, event 11 is File Create, and event 22 is DNS Query. The command line and parent fields in event 1 are what make it useful for behavioural detection.

misconceptions.claim: If the process name is a known Windows binary, the process is legitimate.
misconceptions.correction: Names and paths are trivially copied. Analysts should check the image path, digital signature, hash and parent process. A renamed attacker binary can present the same filename as a system tool.

facts.title: Normalising timestamps before correlation
facts.fact: Logs arrive as RFC 3339 strings, local-time strings, epoch seconds, epoch milliseconds and Windows FILETIME values. Correlation requires one canonical representation, normally UTC in RFC 3339 with a fixed fractional precision. The original string and its offset should be retained alongside the normalized value so a later dispute can be resolved without re-ingesting the source.

references.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: Epoch seconds, epoch milliseconds and 100-nanosecond FILETIME ticks are different units and cannot be compared directly.
Sub-second precision differs by source; mixing millisecond and second precision can reorder events that occurred in the same second.
pitfalls: Storing a timestamp without its offset and later assuming UTC.
Letting a dashboard apply the browser's local zone to a field that was already converted, shifting it twice.

logs.context: Four encodings of the same instant
logs.reading: The first two are unambiguous and equal. The third has no offset and is only 08:14:22 UTC if the source zone is known to be UTC. The fourth is epoch seconds and matches the same instant; treating it as milliseconds would place the event in 1970.

mcqs.question: Which timestamp is unambiguous without any additional context?
mcqs.rationale: The Z suffix states UTC and the ISO 8601 layout is unambiguous. The second lacks an offset, the third lacks a unit, and the fourth is ambiguous between day-first and month-first conventions.

facts.title: Clock skew breaks ordering even when every host uses UTC
facts.fact: Time zones and clock accuracy are different problems. Converting every host to UTC removes offset ambiguity, but a host whose clock is minutes off still writes the wrong instant. Skew distorts event ordering, blows through correlation windows, and can produce authentication failures when Kerberos ticket validation or certificate validity checks disagree with the host clock.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: NTP or a similar service should keep hosts within a small fraction of a second; the acceptable bound is an operational decision.
On Linux, timedatectl and chronyc tracking expose the current offset; on Windows, w32tm /query /status reports the source and last sync.
A collector can flag skew by comparing event time with receipt time and with the host's known offset.
pitfalls: Assuming UTC timestamps are accurate; UTC is a label, not a guarantee that the clock is correct.
Correlating with a window narrower than the observed skew.

logs.context: Same user, two hosts, clocks disagree
logs.text:
2026-11-18T08:14:20Z ws-014.example.internal Security 4624 LogonType=10 TargetUserName=jdoe
2026-11-18T08:18:28Z dc-01.example.internal Security 4771 TargetUserName=jdoe Status=0x18
2026-11-18T08:18:32Z dc-01.example.internal Security 4768 TargetUserName=jdoe
logs.reading: The workstation records the RDP logon at 08:14:20. The domain controller records the Kerberos pre-authentication failure and the TGT request for the same activity at 08:18:28 and 08:18:32. The consistent four-minute offset between the two hosts is clock skew, not a four-minute user delay, and it explains why the failure that preceded the logon appears later in a naive sort.

mcqs.question: Why can clock skew break incident reconstruction even when all logs are stored in UTC?
options: UTC removes offset ambiguity but not the error in each host's clock
UTC cannot represent sub-second precision
UTC timestamps are always written by the collector, not the host
UTC is only valid for Windows hosts
mcqs.rationale: A UTC label says which zone the time is expressed in, not that the underlying clock is correct. A host that is four minutes fast still writes a UTC timestamp that is four minutes wrong.

misconceptions.claim: If every source logs in UTC, events can always be sorted into the correct order.
misconceptions.correction: UTC normalises the offset, but each host's clock can still drift. Ordering also depends on sub-second precision and on whether the timestamp was taken at event time or at ingestion time.

facts.title: Retention and tamper resistance are separate controls
facts.fact: Retention decides how far back an investigation can look; integrity decides whether the retained record can be trusted. NIST SP 800-92 treats log retention as a policy decision driven by operational, legal and regulatory needs rather than a single universal period. Integrity comes from shipping records off the host promptly, restricting who can delete them, using append-only or write-once storage, and enabling controls such as auditd immutable mode.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Central collection shortens the window in which an attacker who owns a host can delete its evidence.
Hashing batches of records or using write-once storage makes later modification detectable.
Retention schedules should distinguish raw events, parsed events and case evidence, which often have different lifetimes.
pitfalls: Treating a long retention period as proof of integrity; a long but editable log is still editable.
Keeping the only copy on the monitored host.

logs.context: auditd switched to immutable mode
logs.text: type=CONFIG_CHANGE msg=audit(1794989662.631:99): op=set audit_enabled=2 old=1 auid=4294967295 ses=4294967295 res=1
logs.reading: The audit configuration is now locked until reboot, so rules cannot be silently weakened. This is an integrity control, but it does not by itself preserve the records; shipping them to a separate collector is still required against an attacker with root.

facts.title: SSH brute force versus failing automation
facts.fact: SSH logs distinguish brute force from automation through pattern rather than any single line. Brute force typically shows many attempts from one source, a rotating list of account names including invalid users, and few or no successes. Automation shows a stable account, a predictable cadence, a public-key or known credential, and often a single retry after a key rotation.

references.title: RFC 4252: The Secure Shell (SSH) Authentication Protocol

details: 'Failed password for invalid user admin' means the account name itself does not exist, which is a strong sign of guessing.
A successful public-key login from a known management subnet on an hourly schedule is usually a deployment or backup job.
Source reputation and whether the source is inside the organisation's own address plan change the interpretation.
pitfalls: Alerting on failure count alone; a stale automation key can produce a steady stream of failures.
Ignoring a success that follows many failures, which is the outcome that matters most.

logs.context: SSH password guessing against one bastion
logs.text:
Nov 18 03:00:01 bastion-01 sshd[2211]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.77 port 51001 ssh2
Nov 18 03:00:02 bastion-01 sshd[2211]: Invalid user test from 203.0.113.77 port 51002
Nov 18 03:00:04 bastion-01 sshd[2211]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 203.0.113.77 port 51003 ssh2
Nov 18 03:00:06 bastion-01 sshd[2211]: error: maximum authentication attempts exceeded for invalid user root from 203.0.113.77 port 51004 ssh2 [preauth]
logs.reading: Four attempts in five seconds, four different account names, all of which do not exist, and a maximum-attempts error. The source 203.0.113.77 is outside the organisation's address plan, and there is no success. This pattern is consistent with automated password guessing.

logs.context: Benign hourly deployment login
logs.text:
Nov 18 02:00:02 bastion-01 sshd[3301]: Failed publickey for svc-deploy from 10.20.30.40 port 40122 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
Nov 18 02:00:03 bastion-01 sshd[3301]: Accepted publickey for svc-deploy from 10.20.30.40 port 40122 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB
logs.reading: Benign: one failure followed by one success, same service account, same management subnet, public-key authentication, and the pair repeats at 02:00 every hour. The failure is the agent trying the previous key during a rotation, not a password guess. The absence of username diversity and the successful key auth clear it.

mcqs.question: Which observation most strongly separates brute force from a failing automation job in SSH logs?
options: Many different account names, including invalid users, from one external source
A single failed attempt followed by a successful public-key login from a management subnet
A login at an unusual hour
A connection that closes before authentication
mcqs.rationale: Username diversity plus invalid accounts plus external origin is the classic guessing pattern. A single retry with a known key from a management network, a login at an odd hour, and a pre-auth disconnect are all individually weak signals.

misconceptions.claim: Any burst of failed SSH logins is an attack.
misconceptions.correction: Automation with an expired or rotated key produces repeated failures from a stable account and source on a regular schedule. The discriminating features are username diversity, source ownership, cadence, authentication method and whether a success follows.

facts.title: Password spraying looks different from brute force
facts.fact: Password spraying tries one or a few common passwords across many accounts to stay under per-account lockout thresholds. The signature is a high count of distinct target accounts from one source with a low number of failures per account, often followed by a success on an account that then behaves unusually. It is easy to miss if the detection groups only by target account.

references.title: 4625(F): An account failed to log on

details: Grouping by source address and counting distinct TargetUserName values exposes the pattern.
Failures are spread over time precisely to avoid lockout, so a per-account threshold may never fire.
The successful account often shows a new source, a new user agent or immediate access to mail or VPN resources.
pitfalls: Tuning only on failures per account, which is the dimension the attacker deliberately keeps low.
Ignoring successful logons from the same source during the spray window.

logs.context: Windows failed logons from one address across many accounts
logs.text:
08:01:02 4625 TargetUserName=ajones    IpAddress=198.51.100.23 LogonType=3 SubStatus=0xc000006a
08:01:09 4625 TargetUserName=bgarcia  IpAddress=198.51.100.23 LogonType=3 SubStatus=0xc000006a
08:01:17 4625 TargetUserName=cmiller  IpAddress=198.51.100.23 LogonType=3 SubStatus=0xc000006a
08:01:25 4625 TargetUserName=dsingh   IpAddress=198.51.100.23 LogonType=3 SubStatus=0xc000006a
08:02:40 4624 TargetUserName=cmiller  IpAddress=198.51.100.23 LogonType=3
logs.reading: Four different accounts fail once each from the same address within 23 seconds, then one of them succeeds. No single account crosses a lockout threshold, but the distinct-account count from one source is the signal. The success on cmiller is the event to scope next.

facts.title: Reading sudo lines: who asked, for what, and as whom
facts.fact: A sudo log line names the invoking user, the terminal, the working directory, the target user and the exact command. The invoking user appears before the colon, while USER= is the account whose privileges were requested. Session open and close lines bracket the command, and auditd's USER_CMD record captures the same action independently when audit rules are in place.
details: TTY=pts/0 indicates an interactive terminal; TTY=? often means a cron job, service or non-interactive session.
A specific command such as /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx is narrower than /bin/bash or sudo -i.
PWD shows where the command ran, which can reveal a script or a suspicious working directory.
pitfalls: Reading USER=root as the person who ran the command; the invoking identity is the field before the colon.
Treating every sudo to a shell as malicious; maintenance and break-glass procedures legitimately do this.

logs.context: sudo command tied to a change window
logs.text:
2026-11-18T09:10:00Z change-api[441]: CHG-2291 approved implementer=jdoe window=09:10-09:30 target=app-01
Nov 18 09:15:02 app-01 sudo:   jdoe : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/jdoe ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
Nov 18 09:15:03 app-01 sudo: pam_unix(sudo:session): session opened for user root by jdoe(uid=1000)
logs.reading: Benign: change CHG-2291 approves jdoe to work on app-01 between 09:10 and 09:30, and at 09:15 jdoe interactively ran one specific service restart as root. The implementing account, the target host and the command all match the approved change, so the sudo event is expected.

logs.context: Non-interactive root shell by a service account
logs.text:
Nov 18 03:12:44 app-01 sudo: svc-backup : TTY=? ; PWD=/var/lib/backup ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash -c 'tar czf /tmp/b.tgz /etc /home'
Nov 18 03:12:44 app-01 sudo: pam_unix(sudo:session): session opened for user root by svc-backup(uid=998)
logs.reading: The invoking account is a backup service, there is no terminal, and the command opens a shell that archives /etc and /home into /tmp. Backups normally read a defined data path, not system configuration and user homes. The combination of service identity, no TTY and broad collection is what makes this worth escalation.

mcqs.question: In a sudo log line, which field identifies the command that was authorised?
options: COMMAND=
USER=
PWD=
TTY=
mcqs.rationale: COMMAND= holds the executed command and its arguments. USER= is the target account whose privileges were requested, PWD= is the working directory, and TTY= is the terminal.

facts.title: Web scanning versus exploitation in access logs
facts.fact: Scanning produces breadth: many paths, mostly missing, with a consistent client and a short interval. Exploitation produces depth: a small number of requests carrying syntax aimed at one parameter, often followed by a response that differs from the baseline. The distinction matters because scanning is noisy but often authorised, while a single successful exploitation request can be quiet.
details: Requests for /.env, /.git/config, /wp-login.php and /actuator/env are enumeration, not exploitation by themselves.
A scanner often identifies itself in the user agent; that string is still client-controlled and must be checked against an allowlist.
Look for a change in response size or status after a payload, not just the presence of the payload.
pitfalls: Calling every 404 storm an incident while missing the one 200 that returned data.
Trusting a scanner user agent without confirming the source address belongs to the scanner.

logs.context: Benign scheduled scanner from an allowlisted address
logs.text:
198.51.100.10 - - [18/Nov/2026:08:15:01 +0000] "GET /.env HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nuclei - Open-source project)"
198.51.100.10 - - [18/Nov/2026:08:15:02 +0000] "GET /.git/config HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nuclei - Open-source project)"
198.51.100.10 - - [18/Nov/2026:08:15:03 +0000] "GET /wp-login.php HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nuclei - Open-source project)"
logs.reading: Benign: every probe returned 404 with the same small body, the source is the vulnerability-management scanner's documented address, and the user agent names the scanner. This is authorised enumeration from the approved scanner. The clearing evidence is the allowlist match plus the absence of any successful or payload-bearing request.

logs.context: Parameter probing that returns data
logs.reading: The first request injects a tautology and gets a 500. Nineteen seconds later a UNION query returns 48 KB instead of the normal 8 KB. The payload, the tool user agent, the error followed by a large 200 response, and the same source together support attempted exploitation with a likely data return.

mcqs.question: A sequence of 404 responses for /.env, /.git/config and /wp-login.php most likely indicates which activity?
options: Path enumeration or scanning
Successful credential theft
A denial-of-service attack
Normal application browsing
mcqs.rationale: These paths are common configuration and administrative targets. Repeated 404s show the requests were made but the files were not served, which is enumeration. Exploitation would require evidence that a request succeeded or changed application behaviour.

facts.title: SQL injection evidence: payload is not proof
facts.fact: A request containing SQL syntax shows an attempt, not a compromise. Confirmation requires a response that differs from the parameterised baseline: extra rows, a database error, a time delay that scales with the payload, or a change in status and size. Applications legitimately receive apostrophes in search terms, and WAF signatures produce false positives on those requests.
details: URL decoding is required before judging a payload; %27 is an apostrophe and %20 is a space.
A generic 500 after a quote can be an application bug rather than a database error.
Time-based evidence needs a control request to show the delay is caused by the payload, not by load.
pitfalls: Matching on the string OR 1=1 without checking whether the request reached a database-backed endpoint.
Ignoring the response body because the access log does not contain it.

logs.context: Benign apostrophe in a search query
logs.reading: Benign: the decoded query is O'Reilly, a book title. The response is 200 with the same size as a normal search page, there is no database error, and the source is an internal client. The apostrophe alone is not injection; the response shows it was handled as a literal search character.

logs.context: Tautology followed by a response-size change
logs.reading: The tautology returns 214 KB while a nonsense control query returns the normal 8 KB. The size difference is the evidence: the first query appears to have returned every row, which is consistent with successful injection. The control request rules out a site-wide layout change.

mcqs.question: Which response pattern is the strongest evidence that a SQL injection attempt succeeded?
options: The response returns a different result set or size that a control request does not reproduce
The server returns HTTP 500 once
The request contains a single quote
The user agent names an injection tool
mcqs.rationale: A reproducible change in returned data, confirmed against a control request, indicates the payload altered the query. A 500, a quote, or a tool user agent shows only that an attempt occurred or that something failed.

misconceptions.claim: Seeing ' OR 1=1 in a URL proves the database was compromised.
misconceptions.correction: It proves a payload was sent. Many requests with SQL syntax are blocked, ignored, or handled by parameterised queries. Confirmation requires evidence that the query changed behaviour, such as extra rows, a database error, or a payload-dependent delay.

facts.title: DNS tunnelling indicators and their benign lookalikes
facts.fact: DNS tunnelling encodes data in query names or response records and relies on DNS being broadly allowed. Indicators include many unique subdomains under one parent, unusually long labels, high-entropy strings, heavy use of TXT or NULL record types, and a regular beacon cadence. The same shape appears in content delivery, antivirus lookups and domain reputation services, so the parent domain and the traffic baseline decide the interpretation.
details: Entropy and label length are weak alone; a single long label can be a legitimate signed token or CDN key.
Count unique subdomains per parent domain per host, not total queries, to see encoding rather than caching.
Response size and record type matter: TXT responses can carry more data than a normal A lookup.
pitfalls: Alerting on any long DNS label; many SaaS and security products use them.
Ignoring the resolver's cache, which can hide repeated lookups from the log.

logs.context: Benign reputation lookups from a security agent
logs.text:
18-Nov-2026 08:14:22.631 client 10.20.30.55#51234: query: 8f3a1c9d2b7e4f60.av-check.example-vendor.test IN A + (72)
18-Nov-2026 08:14:52.640 client 10.20.30.55#51235: query: 1d7b9e4a6c2f8035.av-check.example-vendor.test IN A + (72)
logs.reading: Benign: two lookups per minute, same host, same approved vendor suffix, A records only, and labels are 16 hex characters. This matches the endpoint agent's reputation check. The low volume, fixed domain and lack of TXT traffic distinguish it from a tunnel.

logs.context: High-volume encoded subdomains under one parent
logs.text:
18-Nov-2026 09:10:01.120 client 10.20.30.61#53001: query: a1b2c3d4e5f60718.a94f2c11.t.exfil-example.net IN TXT + (98)
18-Nov-2026 09:10:01.980 client 10.20.30.61#53002: query: 0f9e8d7c6b5a4321.b73e1d02.t.exfil-example.net IN TXT + (98)
18-Nov-2026 09:10:02.840 client 10.20.30.61#53003: query: 5c4b3a291807f6e5.c22d9a43.t.exfil-example.net IN TXT + (98)
logs.reading: Three TXT queries in under two seconds, each with a different high-entropy label and the same parent. The pattern suggests one encoded chunk per query. The parent domain is not on any approved list, and TXT is unusual for ordinary browsing, so this warrants scoping the host and the resolver's response sizes.

facts.title: TLS certificate errors: interception, misconfiguration or expiry
facts.fact: Certificate validation failures include an expired certificate, a name mismatch, an untrusted issuer, a revoked certificate and a weak or unsupported protocol. In a proxy log, the error may describe the client rejecting the proxy's certificate or the proxy rejecting the upstream server's certificate. Internal certificate authorities are common, so an untrusted-issuer error on an internal host is often a trust-store gap rather than interception.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile

details: A hostname mismatch means the certificate is valid for a different name, which can be a misconfiguration or a redirect.
Revocation checking can fail for reasons unrelated to the certificate, such as an unreachable OCSP responder.
Pinned applications may reject a proxy certificate even when the user's browser trusts it.
pitfalls: Concluding that TLS interception is occurring whenever an untrusted-issuer error appears.
Ignoring the direction of the error: client-side and upstream-side failures have different causes.

logs.context: Benign internal CA trust gap
logs.text: 2026-11-18T08:14:22Z proxy-01 tls-inspect[912]: host=legacy.example.internal sni=legacy.example.internal issuer=CN=Example-Internal-CA error=unable to get local issuer certificate action=bypass user=jdoe
logs.reading: Benign: the host is internal, the issuer is the organisation's own CA, and the proxy reports that it lacks the local issuer certificate. The action is a bypass, not a block. This is a trust-store configuration gap on the proxy, not evidence of an attacker intercepting traffic.

logs.context: Self-signed certificate on a rare external host
logs.text: 2026-11-18T09:31:07Z proxy-01 tls-inspect[912]: host=cdn-update.example.net sni=cdn-update.example.net issuer=CN=cdn-update.example.net error=self signed certificate action=allow user=svc-etl bytes_out=48213011
logs.reading: A self-signed certificate on an external host would normally be blocked, but here it was allowed and 48 MB left from a service account. The combination of a rare domain, an untrusted self-signed issuer, an allow decision and a large upload is worth escalating regardless of the certificate error alone.

facts.title: PowerShell -EncodedCommand is common and only sometimes suspicious
facts.fact: PowerShell's -EncodedCommand parameter accepts a Base64 encoding of a UTF-16LE script. Management platforms use it to avoid quoting problems, so its presence alone is weak evidence. What matters is the decoded content, the parent process, the account, whether the script is signed or comes from a known management path, and whether the process makes an unusual network connection.
details: Script block logging, event 4104, records the decoded script text when the policy is enabled.
Process creation event 4688 or Sysmon event 1 records the encoded command line and the parent image.
A management agent such as CcmExec.exe launching PowerShell is expected; a word processor doing so is not.
pitfalls: Decoding as plain Base64 without recognising UTF-16LE, which yields text with interleaved null bytes.
Treating every encoded command as malicious and ignoring the benign management traffic that dominates the volume.

logs.context: Benign management agent invocation
logs.text:
UtcTime: 2026-11-18 06:00:03.112
EventID: 1
Computer: ws-014.example.internal
User: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand RwBlAHQALQBDAGkAbQBJAG4AcwB0AGEAbgBjAGUAIABXAGkAbgAzADIAXwBPAHAAZQByAGEAdABpAG4AZwBTAHkAcwB0AGUAbQA=
ParentImage: C:\Windows\CCM\CcmExec.exe
Signature: Microsoft Windows
SignatureStatus: Valid
logs.reading: Benign: the parent is the Configuration Manager agent, the account is SYSTEM, the invocation is at the fleet's standard 06:00 maintenance time, and the image signature status is Valid. This is the documented software-deployment pattern, not user-driven obfuscation, and the encoded argument decodes to a read-only inventory cmdlet. The decoded script should still match a known signed module for confirmation.

logs.context: Office process spawning encoded PowerShell
logs.text:
UtcTime: 2026-11-18 09:44:18.550
EventID: 1
Computer: ws-022.example.internal
User: EXAMPLE\asmith
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -EncodedCommand <base64 omitted>
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\EXCEL.EXE
logs.reading: Excel spawned a hidden PowerShell with an encoded command. The parent, the hidden window style and the user context are the concerning elements. The next steps are to decode the script, check for a child network connection, and inspect whether a macro or add-in initiated it.

mcqs.question: What encoding does PowerShell's -EncodedCommand parameter expect?
options: Base64 of a UTF-16LE string
Base64 of a UTF-8 string
Hex of an ASCII string
URL encoding of a UTF-8 string
mcqs.rationale: PowerShell decodes the argument from Base64 into UTF-16LE text before execution. Decoding as UTF-8 is a common mistake that produces null-interleaved output.

misconceptions.claim: Base64 in a PowerShell command line is obfuscation and therefore malicious.
misconceptions.correction: EncodedCommand is a supported parameter used by management platforms to avoid quoting issues. Judgement depends on the decoded script, the parent process, the account and the network behaviour, not on the encoding alone.

facts.title: Windows logon type semantics in 4624
facts.fact: Event 4624 records a successful logon and includes LogonType, which describes how the logon was performed. Type 2 is interactive at the console, 3 is network such as SMB or a remote service, 4 is batch, 5 is a service, 7 is unlock, 8 is network with cleartext credentials, 9 is a different credential for the same local session, 10 is remote interactive such as RDP, and 11 is cached interactive. The type changes what the event can tell you about the user's physical or network position.

references.title: 4624(S): An account was successfully logged on
4625(F): An account failed to log on

details: Type 3 is normal for file shares, printers and many service-to-service calls, so it is not inherently suspicious.
Type 10 indicates RDP and is often paired with a source address and a session ID.
Type 9 means the process supplied alternate credentials, and 4648 records the explicit credential use separately.
Event 4672 follows a logon that received administrative privileges and should be read together with 4624.
pitfalls: Treating every type 3 logon as lateral movement; most file access uses type 3.
Reading LogonType without the account, source address and authentication package, which together give the context.

logs.context: Benign service logon over SMB
logs.text:
2026-11-18T07:59:22Z fs-01.example.internal Security 4624 LogonType=3 TargetUserName=svc-backup TargetDomainName=EXAMPLE LogonProcessName=NtLmSsp AuthenticationPackage=NTLM WorkstationName=BACKUP-01 IpAddress=10.20.30.40
2026-11-18T08:14:22Z fs-01.example.internal Security 4624 LogonType=3 TargetUserName=svc-backup TargetDomainName=EXAMPLE LogonProcessName=NtLmSsp AuthenticationPackage=NTLM WorkstationName=BACKUP-01 IpAddress=10.20.30.40
logs.reading: Benign: the same service account logs on over the network from the backup host at 07:59 and again at 08:14, matching a 15-minute backup schedule. Type 3 is expected for SMB, the source is the backup subnet, and the account name matches the job. Nothing here suggests interactive misuse.

logs.context: Network logon from a workstation to a server
logs.text: 2026-11-18T09:02:11Z fs-01.example.internal Security 4624 LogonType=3 TargetUserName=jdoe TargetDomainName=EXAMPLE LogonProcessName=NtLmSsp AuthenticationPackage=NTLM WorkstationName=WS-022 IpAddress=10.20.30.61
logs.reading: A user logon over NTLM from a workstation to a file server can be ordinary mapped-drive access. It becomes interesting when the same workstation authenticates to many servers in a short period, or when it is followed by 4672 on a server the user does not administer.

mcqs.question: Which Windows logon type indicates a network logon such as an SMB connection?
options: Type 3
Type 2
Type 5
Type 10
mcqs.rationale: Type 3 is network, type 2 is interactive at the console, type 5 is a service logon, and type 10 is remote interactive, typically RDP.

misconceptions.claim: Logon type 3 always means lateral movement.
misconceptions.correction: Type 3 covers ordinary network authentication such as file shares, printer access and service calls. Lateral movement is suggested by the combination of an unusual account, many targets, privileged follow-on events, or a source that does not normally authenticate that way.

facts.title: Reading Kubernetes audit verbs and subresources
facts.fact: Kubernetes audit records express the action as an HTTP verb plus an object reference. A get on a secret is a read of that object, while create on pods/exec is how an exec session into a container appears. Identity is in user.username, the caller's address is in sourceIPs, and the outcome is in responseStatus.code. Namespace and RBAC scope determine whether the action is expected.

references.title: Kubernetes API server audit configuration v1

details: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> identifies a workload identity, not a human.
A 403 response is a denied attempt and can still be valuable evidence of probing.
list and watch are common for controllers and monitoring agents and are usually high volume.
pitfalls: Assuming an exec event means a shell succeeded; check responseStatus and the subresource.
Ignoring cross-namespace access when the identity's RBAC role is namespace-scoped.

logs.context: Benign monitoring list operation
logs.text: {"kind":"Event","apiVersion":"audit.k8s.io/v1","level":"Metadata","stage":"ResponseComplete","verb":"list","user":{"username":"system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus"},"sourceIPs":["10.20.30.77"],"objectRef":{"resource":"pods","namespace":"monitoring","apiVersion":"v1"},"responseStatus":{"code":200},"requestReceivedTimestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z"}
logs.reading: Benign: the monitoring service account lists pods in its own namespace, from the monitoring node, with a 200. This is the expected discovery pattern for a metrics collector and matches its RBAC scope.

logs.context: Service account reading a secret in another namespace
logs.text: {"kind":"Event","apiVersion":"audit.k8s.io/v1","level":"RequestResponse","stage":"ResponseComplete","verb":"get","user":{"username":"system:serviceaccount:reporting:etl-runner"},"sourceIPs":["10.20.30.77"],"objectRef":{"resource":"secrets","namespace":"payments","name":"db-creds","apiVersion":"v1"},"responseStatus":{"code":200},"requestReceivedTimestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z"}
logs.reading: A reporting identity read payment database credentials and received 200. The namespace crossing is the key fact: unless the ETL job is documented to use that secret, this is either an RBAC design flaw or credential access by a compromised workload.

mcqs.question: A Kubernetes audit event shows verb=get and objectRef.resource=secrets. What does this indicate?
options: A read of a secret object, which must be judged against the caller's identity and RBAC scope
A secret was created
The API server denied the request automatically
The caller executed a shell in a pod
mcqs.rationale: get is a read. Creation would be create, denial would show a 403 responseStatus, and exec appears as create on the pods/exec subresource.

facts.title: Cloud storage access patterns: backup versus collection
facts.fact: Object storage access is easy to log at volume and easy to misread. A backup job reads or writes a predictable prefix with a stable role, a schedule and a consistent user agent. Collection activity tends to enumerate buckets, read many distinct keys across prefixes, use an unusual identity or user agent, and may show AccessDenied errors while probing. The identity and the key pattern matter more than the raw count.

references.title: CloudTrail record contents for management, data, and network activity events
Logging Amazon S3 API calls using AWS CloudTrail

details: ListBucket followed by many GetObject calls is a common discovery-then-collect sequence.
A role session name often encodes the job or date and can corroborate the expected schedule.
Cross-account access and public bucket policy changes deserve separate, higher-severity treatment.
pitfalls: Alerting only on object count; a legitimate restore can read thousands of objects.
Assuming the source address is the user's location when an AWS service made the call on their behalf.

logs.context: Benign nightly backup read
logs.text: {"eventTime":"2026-11-18T02:00:04Z","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com","eventName":"GetObject","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.50","userAgent":"aws-cli/2.15.0","userIdentity":{"type":"AssumedRole","arn":"arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/backup-runner/backup-20261118"},"requestParameters":{"bucketName":"example-backups","key":"db/2026/11/18/full.tar.gz"}}
logs.reading: Benign: the role is backup-runner, the session name contains the date, the key matches the nightly full-backup prefix, and the call occurs at 02:00 as scheduled. The pattern is stable and documented.

logs.context: Enumeration followed by broad object reads
logs.text:
{"eventTime":"2026-11-18T09:14:02Z","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com","eventName":"ListBucket","sourceIPAddress":"198.51.100.61","userAgent":"python-requests/2.31","userIdentity":{"type":"IAMUser","arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/contractor-07"},"requestParameters":{"bucketName":"example-customer-exports"}}
{"eventTime":"2026-11-18T09:14:40Z","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com","eventName":"GetObject","sourceIPAddress":"198.51.100.61","userAgent":"python-requests/2.31","userIdentity":{"type":"IAMUser","arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/contractor-07"},"requestParameters":{"bucketName":"example-customer-exports","key":"2026/09/exports-part-017.csv"}}
logs.reading: A contractor identity lists a customer-exports bucket, then reads a numbered part file with a generic Python user agent from an external address. Enumeration plus part-file reads is a collection pattern; verify the contractor's engagement and whether the bucket policy should allow that identity at all.

mcqs.question: Which CloudTrail field identifies the IAM principal that made an API call?
options: userIdentity.arn
sourceIPAddress
eventSource
awsRegion
mcqs.rationale: userIdentity describes the principal, including its type and ARN. sourceIPAddress is the network origin, eventSource names the service, and awsRegion is the endpoint region.

facts.title: Clearing an alert needs a positive explanation
facts.fact: An alert is cleared as benign when there is a specific, evidence-backed reason the activity is expected, not merely because no malicious indicator was found. The explanation should name the actor, the business process, the expected timing and the control that corroborates it. If the only support is 'nothing else looked bad', the alert is better left open or escalated than closed as a false positive.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Corroboration can come from a change ticket, an asset owner, a scheduled job, a baseline, or an independent log source.
The explanation should be reproducible by another analyst from the case notes.
Absence of malware on disk does not explain why an encoded command ran.
pitfalls: Using 'known good' as a reason without recording what makes it known good.
Closing an alert because the user is senior or the host is internal.

logs.context: Nightly updatedb process on a database host
logs.text:
2026-11-18T03:00:01Z db-02.example.internal audit: type=SYSCALL msg=audit(1794980401.002:7781): arch=c000003e syscall=59 success=yes exit=0 ppid=22990 pid=22991 auid=4294967295 uid=0 gid=0 euid=0 comm="updatedb" exe="/usr/bin/updatedb" key="exec"
2026-11-18T03:00:01Z db-02.example.internal cron[22990]: (root) CMD (/usr/bin/updatedb --prunepaths=/var/lib/postgresql)
logs.reading: Benign: the cron record shows root launching updatedb at 03:00 with an explicit prune path, and the audit record shows the same process with a matching parent. The job is documented, runs nightly, and touches no unexpected path. The cron line is the positive explanation that clears the audit alert.

mcqs.question: What is the minimum standard for closing an alert as benign?
options: A specific benign explanation supported by corroborating evidence
No malware was found on the host
The user has a senior job title
The alert came from an internal address
mcqs.rationale: A benign closure should name the expected activity and support it with evidence such as a schedule, ticket, owner confirmation, or independent log. The other options are assumptions that do not explain the observed behaviour.

misconceptions.claim: If no malware hash is found, the alert is a false positive.
misconceptions.correction: Absence of a known hash only means the sample is not in that hash set. The activity still needs an explanation. Living-off-the-land techniques often use signed system binaries with no malicious file at all.

facts.title: Severity is not priority
facts.fact: Severity is the technical weight a detection assigns to an event, usually from the rule. Priority is the order in which the organisation should work, and it adds asset criticality, identity privilege, data sensitivity, exposure and current threat context. A high-severity rule on an isolated test host can be low priority, while a medium-severity identity event on a domain controller can be urgent.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Priority should be computed from severity plus context, not copied from the rule level.
A single rule can produce different priorities for different assets and identities.
Queue order should be visible to analysts so they can see why one case outranks another.
pitfalls: Sorting the queue by rule severity alone and starving high-impact medium alerts.
Letting priority inflate permanently because an asset was once critical.

logs.context: Alert with severity and computed priority
logs.text: {"alert_id":"ALRT-2026-11842","rule":"SSH authentication failure burst","severity":"high","asset":{"host":"lab-07","tier":"test","owner":"engineering"},"identity":{"user":"testuser","privileged":false},"priority":"P4","reason":"isolated test host with no production credentials"}
logs.reading: The rule severity is high because the failure count crossed its threshold, but the asset is an isolated test host with an unprivileged test account. The computed priority is P4. Severity describes the pattern; priority describes the consequence of ignoring it.

mcqs.question: Which factor most directly raises an alert's priority without changing the rule's severity?
options: The affected asset is a tier-one production system
The rule has more than one condition
The alert was generated at night
The log source uses JSON
mcqs.rationale: Priority incorporates business and asset context. A tier-one system raises consequence while the rule's technical severity stays the same. Rule structure, time of day and log format do not by themselves change impact.

facts.title: Alert enrichment: asset, identity and threat context
facts.fact: Enrichment adds the context needed to judge an alert: asset owner and criticality, whether an identity is active, disabled or privileged, the source's ASN and geography, threat-intelligence verdicts, recent related alerts, and exposure from vulnerability data. Good enrichment is fast, cached and explicit about failures, because a blank field caused by a timeout must not be read as 'no data found'.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Identity context should include employment status and role, not just a display name.
Asset context should include owner, environment, data classification and whether the host is internet-facing.
Threat-intelligence hits need a confidence and freshness value; a decade-old indicator is weak evidence.
pitfalls: Treating a failed enrichment lookup as a negative result.
Using stale HR data so a terminated employee still appears active.

logs.context: Alert enriched with identity and asset context
logs.text: {"alert_id":"ALRT-2026-11901","user":{"name":"jdoe","department":"finance","status":"active","privileged":false},"asset":{"host":"fs-01","criticality":"tier-1","owner":"payments","internet_facing":false},"src_ip":{"asn":64500,"country":"NL"},"intel":{"verdict":"unknown","confidence":"none"},"related_alerts_7d":3}
logs.reading: The identity is an active, non-privileged finance user, the target is a tier-one payments file server, and the source is an unfamiliar foreign ASN. The unknown intelligence verdict is explicitly recorded as unknown rather than treated as clean. This context supports escalation without asserting that the IP is malicious.

facts.title: A repeatable triage checklist
facts.fact: Triage should follow a fixed sequence so that analysts do not skip scope under time pressure. A practical order is: confirm the alert came from real data and the right rule; identify the asset, identity and time window; establish what succeeded versus failed; scope related hosts, accounts and addresses; corroborate with an independent source; assess business impact; then decide to close, escalate or contain. Every step should leave a note.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Validate the detection itself first, including parser errors and stale data, before investigating the actor.
Separate attempted from successful actions; a failed logon and a created process are different severities of fact.
Record the negative findings too, so the next analyst knows what was already excluded.
pitfalls: Starting containment before scope, which can destroy the evidence needed to size the incident.
Accepting the alert's own summary as the timeline instead of checking raw events.

logs.context: Alert record to be triaged
logs.text: {"alert":"Impossible travel","user":"jdoe","events":[{"ts":"2026-11-18T07:02:11Z","geo":"NL","result":"success"},{"ts":"2026-11-18T07:41:52Z","geo":"SG","result":"success"}],"mfa":"satisfied","client":"browser"}
logs.reading: Two successful browser logons 39 minutes apart from the Netherlands and Singapore with MFA satisfied. Before treating it as impossible travel, check whether the user is on a corporate VPN with an egress in one location, whether both events share a device identifier, and whether the identity provider records a single session. The MFA result and client type are part of the scope step.

mcqs.question: After confirming that an alert reflects real data, what should triage establish next?
options: The scope: affected assets, identities, addresses and time window
Whether the user has a LinkedIn profile
The rule author's name
The SIEM licence tier
mcqs.rationale: Scope determines whether the event is isolated or part of a wider incident and drives every later decision. Rule authorship and licence tier are not investigative facts, and open-source profiling is not a substitute for internal evidence.

facts.title: Escalation criteria that do not depend on gut feeling
facts.fact: Escalation should be triggered by observable conditions: confirmed code execution, access by a privileged or service identity, data access or transfer, persistence, activity on multiple hosts, communication with an untrusted external endpoint, or involvement of regulated data. The criteria should say who is notified, within what time, and what the analyst must hand over. Escalation is not the same as containment; it brings in the people who can authorise it.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: A privileged group change, a new service, or a scheduled task on a server are common escalation triggers even without malware.
The escalation note should include scope, evidence, actions already taken and the specific question for the next tier.
Regulatory and contractual notification clocks may start before technical confirmation, so legal counsel is a parallel path.
pitfalls: Escalating everything, which defeats the purpose of a tiered model.
Waiting for certainty before escalating a confirmed privileged compromise.

logs.context: Privileged group membership change
logs.text: 2026-11-18T09:02:11Z ws-014.example.internal Security 4728 MemberName=CN=svc-backup,OU=Service Accounts,DC=example,DC=internal GroupName=Domain Admins SubjectUserName=helpdesk-02 SubjectDomainName=EXAMPLE
