logs.reading: A helpdesk account added a backup service account to Domain Admins. Adding a service account to the highest privilege group is a clear escalation trigger: it changes the identity's blast radius, may be unauthorised, and needs the directory owner to confirm the change request.

mcqs.question: Which finding most clearly requires immediate escalation?
options: A helpdesk account added a service account to Domain Admins
A user mistyped a password once
A workstation installed a signed browser update
A laptop connected to the guest wireless network
mcqs.rationale: Adding an account to a highly privileged group is a durable privilege change with broad impact, and the actor and change record must be verified. The other events are common and low impact on their own.

facts.title: Containment thresholds and reversible action
facts.fact: Containment is a trade-off between stopping spread and preserving business function and evidence. A host with confirmed malicious execution and outbound command-and-control traffic is a strong candidate for network isolation; a single low-confidence alert on a business-critical system may justify monitoring, credential reset or blocking one destination first. The decision should record confidence, blast radius, business impact and the approval authority.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Prefer reversible actions first: block a destination, revoke a session, disable one account, then isolate the host.
Preserve volatile evidence such as memory and active connections before powering off or wiping.
Isolation can tip off an attacker, so coordinate with the investigation lead when the actor may still be active.
Document the exact action and time, because containment changes the evidence available later.
pitfalls: Isolating every alerted host by default, which trains the business to resist security action.
Shutting a machine down before collecting memory and volatile network state.

logs.context: EDR containment action record
logs.text: {"ts":"2026-11-18T09:40:12Z","action":"isolate_host","host":"ws-014.example.internal","actor":"analyst-3","case":"CASE-2026-0412","approval":"IR-LEAD","result":"success","note":"memory captured before isolation"}
logs.reading: The record shows who isolated the host, when, under which case, with which approval, and that memory was captured first. That is the documentation a containment threshold needs: the action is attributable, authorised and ordered correctly relative to evidence collection.

mcqs.question: Before isolating a suspected compromised host, which action best preserves evidence?
options: Capture memory and active network connections first
Reboot the host to clear any malicious processes
Run a full antivirus scan and delete detected files
Delete temporary files to reduce the investigation scope
mcqs.rationale: Memory and live connections disappear on reboot or shutdown. Isolation itself may be appropriate, but volatile state should be captured first when compromise is suspected, and the action and time recorded.

misconceptions.claim: The correct first response is always to isolate the host immediately.
misconceptions.correction: Isolation is one option whose cost depends on confidence, spread risk, business criticality and evidence needs. Premature isolation can destroy volatile evidence and disrupt services without improving safety, so the threshold should be explicit.

facts.title: Case notes that another analyst can use
facts.fact: Case documentation should be contemporaneous, factual and reproducible. Record the alert, the scope, the evidence reviewed with timestamps in UTC, the actions taken and their results, the decisions and the alternatives considered. Avoid conclusions without the supporting observation, and distinguish what was verified from what was inferred.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Quote exact event fields or attach the query, not a paraphrase of what the log 'basically said'.
Record negative results and dead ends; they prevent duplicated work on the next shift.
Note any evidence that was not collected and why, such as a host that was offline.
pitfalls: Writing a narrative that omits timestamps, making the timeline impossible to reconstruct.
Storing evidence only in chat messages that will be lost or edited.

mcqs.question: Which entry makes a case note reproducible by another analyst?
options: The exact query, time range and UTC timestamps used
A summary that says the activity looked suspicious
The analyst's opinion of the user's intent
A screenshot with no source or collection time
mcqs.rationale: Reproducibility requires the query, scope and timestamps so another analyst can re-run the same search. Opinions and context-free screenshots cannot be verified or extended.

facts.title: Structured shift handoff
facts.fact: A shift handoff should transfer state, not just greetings. It covers open incidents and their current status, the next action and owner, recent closures with the reason, watchlist items that are not yet alerts, pending approvals, and the health of the detection pipeline. A written handoff with case links is safer than a verbal summary because it survives interruptions and can be audited.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Include what changed since the last shift, especially new suppressions or data-source outages.
Flag cases that will breach an SLA during the next shift.
Hand off hypotheses and hunches as explicit watch items, not as conclusions.
pitfalls: A verbal handoff that leaves no record of pending actions.
Handing off a case without saying which step was already completed.

mcqs.question: Which item belongs in a structured shift handoff?
options: Open cases with status, next action and owner
Only the number of tickets closed during the shift
A list of every detection rule deployed in the SIEM
The analyst's personal assessment of each colleague
mcqs.rationale: A handoff transfers state: what is open, what happens next, who owns it, and what is pending. Ticket counts alone do not tell the next shift what to do, and rule inventories are reference material rather than case state.

misconceptions.claim: A verbal handoff at the end of a shift is sufficient if the team is small.
misconceptions.correction: Verbal handoffs lose detail and leave no auditable record. Even a short written summary with case identifiers and next actions prevents duplicated work and dropped follow-ups, and it is essential when the next shift is remote or in another time zone.

facts.title: False positives, benign true positives and noise
facts.fact: Not every closed alert is a false positive. A false positive means the detection logic fired incorrectly, for example a parser mapped the wrong field. A benign true positive means the activity really occurred and the rule correctly described it, but the activity is expected. Environmental noise is a third category, such as a scanner that is authorised but not excluded. Each needs a different fix.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: A parser bug needs a pipeline fix, not a suppression.
An expected business activity needs an allowlist with an owner and an expiry date.
Tracking reason codes by rule shows whether tuning is working or just hiding volume.
pitfalls: Using 'false positive' as a single bin for every non-incident, which hides fixable data problems.
Suppressing a rule permanently because of one noisy environment.

logs.context: Benign administrative logon from the corporate VPN
logs.text:
2026-11-18T07:58:03Z vpn-01 openvpn[812]: jdoe/203.0.113.21:51820 Peer Connection Initiated
2026-11-18T07:58:09Z ws-014.example.internal Security 4624 LogonType=10 TargetUserName=jdoe IpAddress=203.0.113.21 AuthenticationPackage=Negotiate
logs.reading: Benign true positive: six seconds after a VPN session for jdoe, an RDP logon for the same account arrives from the address the VPN assigned. The source is the corporate VPN pool rather than the internet, and the rule correctly detected remote interactive logon; the activity is expected. The fix is to scope the rule to external or non-VPN sources, not to call the detection broken.

facts.title: Alert fatigue is a measurement problem
facts.fact: Alert fatigue is not simply 'too many alerts'. It is the condition where the volume of low-value alerts reduces the probability that a real one is investigated. The useful measure is the actionable ratio: how many alerts lead to a meaningful action or confirmed finding. Deduplication, entity grouping, risk-based queueing and expiring suppressions reduce volume without hiding signal; blanket threshold increases do not.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Group alerts by entity and time so one noisy host does not produce fifty queue items.
Track how often analysts close without reading the evidence, a direct symptom of fatigue.
Automate enrichment and case creation, but do not automate the decision to ignore.
pitfalls: Raising every threshold until the queue is quiet, which also removes the true positives.
Measuring only alert count and not the proportion that were actionable.

logs.context: Weekly rule volume with suppression counts
logs.text:
rule=ssh_auth_failure_burst generated=412 suppressed=380 escalated=6 benign=26
rule=new_local_admin generated=9 suppressed=0 escalated=4 benign=5
rule=encoded_powershell generated=57 suppressed=41 escalated=3 benign=13
logs.reading: The SSH rule produced 412 alerts but 380 were suppressed and only 6 escalated, so its unsuppressed actionable yield is low and the suppression logic deserves review. The local-admin rule produced only 9 alerts but 4 escalations, a much higher yield. Volume alone would rank the wrong rule first.

mcqs.question: Which metric best captures alert fatigue in a SOC queue?
options: The proportion of alerts that lead to a meaningful action or confirmed finding
The total number of alerts generated per day
The number of rules deployed
The average length of an analyst's shift
mcqs.rationale: Actionable ratio measures signal yield rather than raw volume. A large alert count can be healthy if most are actionable, and a small count can still be fatiguing if almost none are.

misconceptions.claim: Alert fatigue is solved by raising thresholds until the queue is manageable.
misconceptions.correction: Blanket threshold increases suppress true positives along with noise. Fatigue is better addressed by removing duplicate alerts, grouping by entity, fixing parser errors, adding owned and expiring allowlists, and measuring actionable yield.

facts.title: Validating detections with known-bad and known-good cases
facts.fact: A detection is validated when it fires on representative malicious activity and stays quiet on representative benign activity, using the same pipeline that production uses. Purple-team exercises, atomic tests and replayed historical events provide the positive cases; production baselines and approved business activity provide the negative cases. A rule that passes only a hand-written fixture has demonstrated syntax, not coverage.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Run the test through the real parser and field mapping, not against the raw fixture alone.
Record the expected alert fields, not just whether an alert appeared.
Re-validate after log-source upgrades, because a field rename can silently break the match.
pitfalls: Testing with a fixture that contains fields production never populates.
Counting a rule as validated because it once fired in production; that may have been a false positive.

logs.context: Positive test fixture for a failed-logon rule
logs.text: {"@timestamp":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z","event":{"code":"4625","outcome":"failure"},"host":{"name":"ws-014"},"user":{"name":"jdoe"},"source":{"ip":"203.0.113.77"},"winlog":{"event_data":{"LogonType":"3","SubStatus":"0xc000006a"}}}
logs.reading: This fixture represents a known-bad network logon failure with the fields the rule references. A validation run should confirm that the rule fires and that the alert carries ws-014, jdoe and the source address. The companion negative fixture should use a successful logon and confirm silence.

mcqs.question: What does a passing unit test on a detection rule prove?
options: The rule matches the supplied fixture through the tested pipeline
The rule detects every real-world variant of the technique
The rule has no false positives in production
The rule is mapped to the correct ATT&CK technique
mcqs.rationale: A unit test proves behaviour on the fixture and pipeline used. It does not establish production coverage, false-positive rate, or correct technique mapping, which need separate validation and review.

facts.title: MTTD, MTTA and MTTR: definitions before dashboards
facts.fact: Mean time to detect, acknowledge and respond are only comparable when their start and stop points are defined. Detection might start at the first event or at the alert; acknowledgement at the first analyst action; response at containment or closure. Means are easily skewed by a few long cases, so medians and percentiles usually describe the queue better. Metrics should distinguish detection quality from staffing delay.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: A fast MTTA can coexist with a slow MTTD if the alert was late; the two measure different stages.
Percentiles such as p50 and p90 expose the tail that a mean hides.
Changing the definition mid-quarter makes trend comparisons meaningless.
pitfalls: Optimising MTTR by closing cases earlier rather than resolving them.
Comparing metrics across organisations with different definitions.

mcqs.question: Why are medians often preferred over means for SOC response-time metrics?
options: A few very long cases can pull the mean away from the typical experience
Medians are required by NIST
Means cannot be calculated for timestamps
Medians include weekends and means do not
mcqs.rationale: Response-time distributions are skewed by a small number of long-running incidents. The median describes the typical case, while the mean is inflated by the tail. Reporting percentiles as well gives a fuller picture.

facts.title: Anatomy of a Sigma rule
facts.fact: A Sigma rule is YAML with metadata and a detection block. Metadata includes title, a UUID id, status, description, author, references, tags and level. The logsource block selects a category, product or service. The detection block defines named selections and a condition that combines them, and falsepositives documents known benign causes. Sigma is vendor-neutral, so a backend pipeline translates its field names into the target SIEM's schema.
details: The condition can use and, or, not and one or more of them, with parentheses for grouping.
tags commonly include attack.<tactic> and attack.t<technique> for ATT&CK mapping.
status values such as experimental, test and stable communicate review maturity.
pitfalls: Assuming a Sigma rule runs unchanged in every SIEM; field names and modifiers need a translation pipeline.
Leaving falsepositives empty, which hides known noise from the reviewer.

configs.snippet:
title: SSH Authentication Failure Burst
id: 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111
status: experimental
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: sshd
detection:
  selection:
    message|contains: 'Failed password for'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Automation using an expired key
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1110
configs.purpose: Minimal Sigma rule showing metadata, logsource, detection, condition, false positives and ATT&CK tags.

mcqs.question: In Sigma, which section maps a rule to the type of log source it expects?
options: logsource
detection
falsepositives
tags
mcqs.rationale: logsource declares category, product or service. detection holds the selections and condition, falsepositives documents benign causes, and tags carry classification such as ATT&CK.

facts.title: Sigma field modifiers change matching semantics
facts.fact: Modifiers are appended to a field name with a pipe and alter how its values are compared. contains, startswith and endswith do substring matching; all changes a list from OR to AND; re applies a regular expression; cidr matches network ranges; base64offset handles encoded strings whose alignment varies; windash matches common Windows dash variants; fieldref compares one field to another. Modifiers can be chained, and their order matters.
details: A plain list of values under one field is OR; adding all makes every value required.
base64offset produces several variants because base64 encoding depends on the byte offset of the substring.
windash covers hyphen, en dash and other dash characters that command-line parsers may accept.
pitfalls: Using contains on a very short string, which over-matches unrelated commands.
Assuming modifier order is irrelevant when chaining, for example base64offset and contains.

configs.snippet:
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '-enc'
      - '-nop'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'FromBase64String'
      - 'DownloadString'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flags and selection_payload
configs.purpose: Combine image matching, multiple required flags and payload keywords without writing a regular expression.

mcqs.question: What does the Sigma |all modifier change about a list of values?
options: It requires every listed value to match instead of any one
It makes the match case-sensitive
It base64-encodes each value
It limits the match to the first value
mcqs.rationale: By default values are ORed. all switches the list to AND, so a command line must contain each listed token. Case sensitivity is a separate concern of the backend, and encoding is handled by base64 modifiers.

misconceptions.claim: A Sigma rule's field names are universal, so the same YAML works in every SIEM.
misconceptions.correction: Sigma is a vendor-neutral specification. Backends use different schemas, so a conversion pipeline maps abstract fields such as Image or CommandLine onto the target's fields. Without that mapping a rule may run but match nothing.

facts.title: KQL: the pipe, where and summarize
facts.fact: Kusto Query Language composes a query as a pipeline. A tabular expression starts with a table such as SecurityEvent, then each pipe passes rows to the next operator. where filters, summarize aggregates with functions such as count and dcount, bin groups timestamps into fixed buckets, and by names the grouping keys. The result is a table, so operators can be added or removed without rewriting the whole query.
details: Time filters should be explicit, for example where TimeGenerated > ago(24h), rather than relying on the portal's default.
dcount counts distinct values, which is how you measure account or host diversity.
Join and union combine tables but multiply or merge rows, so check cardinality before alerting.
pitfalls: Forgetting that string comparisons may be case-sensitive depending on the operator and column type.
Using summarize without a time bin, which collapses the whole period into one row and hides bursts.

configs.snippet:
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Failures >= 20
| order by Failures desc
configs.purpose: Count failed logons per source address in ten-minute buckets and keep the busiest windows.

logs.context: Output rows from the failed-logon query
logs.reading: The external address produced 41 failures across three accounts in one ten-minute bucket, then 37 more in the next. The internal management address produced two failures for one account, which is consistent with a key retry. The Accounts column adds the diversity signal that raw counts lack.

mcqs.question: Which KQL pattern produces per-entity counts in fixed time buckets?
options: summarize count() by Entity, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
where Entity == 'x'
project Entity, TimeGenerated
join kind=inner (OtherTable) on Entity
mcqs.rationale: summarize applies an aggregate such as count, and the by clause groups by entity and by a binned timestamp. where filters, project selects columns, and join combines tables but does not bucket.

facts.title: SPL: search, stats and field extraction
facts.fact: Splunk's search processing language starts with a search that selects an index and often a sourcetype, then pipes results through commands. stats computes aggregates such as count and dc, eval creates fields, rex extracts with a regular expression, and tstats queries accelerated summaries when available. Field names depend on the sourcetype and on configured extractions, so a query that works on one feed may need adjustment on another.
details: index and sourcetype narrow the search before any expensive command runs.
dc(field) counts distinct values, which is useful for account or host diversity.
tstats is much faster than raw search but only covers fields present in the data model or accelerated summary.
pitfalls: Using a raw search over all indexes and relying on the time picker to keep it cheap.
Assuming a field exists because it appears in the raw text; it may need an explicit extraction.

configs.snippet:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password"
| rex field=_raw "from (?<src_ip>\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})"
| stats count AS failures dc(user) AS accounts BY src_ip
| where failures > 20
| sort - failures
configs.purpose: Extract the source address from SSH failures and rank sources by failure count and account diversity.

logs.context: Result table from the SPL search
logs.text:
src_ip          failures  accounts
203.0.113.77    78        3
10.20.30.40     2         1
logs.reading: The external source accounts for 78 failures across three usernames, while the internal address shows the single-account retry pattern. The stats command has already reduced thousands of raw lines to two rows, which is the point of aggregating before alerting.

mcqs.question: In SPL, which command calculates aggregate statistics such as counts grouped by a field?
options: stats
rex
eval
table
mcqs.rationale: stats performs aggregation with functions such as count and dc and a BY clause. rex extracts fields, eval computes new fields per row, and table only selects and orders columns.

facts.title: Threshold rules and correlation rules answer different questions
facts.fact: A threshold rule aggregates events of one type and fires when a count crosses a limit inside a window, for example more than twenty failed logons per source in ten minutes. A correlation rule combines different event types or a sequence, for example a failure followed by a success from the same source and account. Correlation carries state and ordering, so window semantics, late-arriving events, entity keys and duplicate suppression determine whether it behaves correctly.
details: Tumbling windows do not overlap; sliding windows do, and can count the same event in several evaluations.
A sequence rule should define whether order is required and how far apart the steps may occur.
Late events can arrive after the window closed, so a correlation engine needs a grace period or a re-evaluation strategy.
Entity keys must be normalized, or the same host written two ways will never join.
pitfalls: Using a threshold when the behaviour is defined by sequence; volume alone cannot express 'failure then success'.
Ignoring duplicate ingestion, which inflates counts and can fire a threshold on one real event.

mcqs.question: A rule fires when a failed logon is followed by a successful logon from the same address within ten minutes. What kind of rule is this?
options: A correlation rule with sequence and time constraints
A simple threshold rule on failed-logon count
A static blocklist match
A vulnerability signature
mcqs.rationale: The rule combines two event types, requires an order, and constrains the interval, which is correlation. A threshold would only count failures and would miss the success that gives the pattern its meaning.

misconceptions.claim: A correlation rule that works in testing will behave the same at production volume.
misconceptions.correction: Production adds late events, duplicates, retries and clock skew. Window boundaries and join keys that looked clean in a small sample can produce missed pairs or repeated alerts at scale, so correlation rules need volume testing and monitoring of unmatched or dropped events.

facts.title: Tuning against a baseline without overfitting
facts.fact: Tuning compares a rule's output with what is normal for each environment. A baseline can be deterministic, such as an inventory of approved scanners, or statistical, such as the usual number of failed logons per host per hour. Good tuning is scoped, owned and time-limited; it records why an exception exists and when it should be reviewed. Overfitting produces a rule that is quiet only because it has learned the current noise, including the attacker's.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: Baselines should account for weekday and weekend patterns, maintenance windows and seasonal business cycles.
An allowlist entry should name an owner, a justification and an expiry or review date.
Measure the effect of tuning on both false positives and missed true positives, not just volume.
pitfalls: Excluding an entire subnet because one host was noisy.
Tuning until the rule no longer fires on the attack it was written for.

configs.snippet:
exceptions:
  - id: EXC-0042
    scope: source.ip = 198.51.100.10
    reason: Authorised vulnerability scanner
    owner: security-testing@example.internal
    expires: 2027-01-31
configs.purpose: Record a scoped, owned and expiring tuning exception instead of an untracked filter.

misconceptions.claim: A well-tuned rule should produce no false positives.
misconceptions.correction: Some false positives are unavoidable when detection depends on probabilistic behaviour, and driving them to zero usually costs detection coverage. The goal is a managed, measured rate with documented exceptions, not silence.

facts.title: Mapping detections to MITRE ATT&CK
facts.fact: ATT&CK mapping connects a detection to the adversary behaviour it observes, using a tactic and a technique or sub-technique identifier. It helps communicate coverage, find gaps and prioritise hunts, but it does not prove that a rule detects the technique in all its forms. A single rule can cover several techniques, and one technique usually needs several rules across different data sources.
details: Use sub-techniques where the behaviour is specific, for example T1059.001 for PowerShell.
Record the data sources a technique requires; a missing log source is a coverage gap regardless of rule count.
ATT&CK versions change, so mappings should be reviewed when the matrix is updated.
pitfalls: Counting one rule per technique as complete coverage.
Mapping by tool name rather than by observed behaviour.

mcqs.question: What does mapping a detection rule to T1059.001 communicate?
options: The rule targets PowerShell execution behaviour, not that coverage is complete
The rule detects every ATT&CK technique
The rule is guaranteed free of false positives
The rule was approved by MITRE
mcqs.rationale: The tag associates the rule with the PowerShell sub-technique. It says nothing about completeness, false-positive rate or endorsement; coverage still depends on data sources and variants.

facts.title: Detection rules belong in version control with tests
facts.fact: Detection-as-code treats rules like software: stored in a repository, reviewed by peers, validated in continuous integration, deployed through a pipeline and versioned for rollback. Validation should include schema checks, translation to each backend, and unit tests with positive and negative fixtures. The pipeline should fail closed when a rule cannot be translated, rather than deploying a rule that silently matches nothing.
details: A pull request should show the rule diff, the test fixtures and the expected alert fields.
Backend translation should be tested for every SIEM in use, not just the primary one.
Deployment metadata should record who approved the rule and which data sources it assumes.
pitfalls: Testing only that the YAML parses; a valid rule can still be logically wrong.
Letting rules drift between the repository and the live SIEM with manual edits.

commands.code:
sigma check rules/ssh_failure_burst.yml
sigma convert -t splunk rules/ssh_failure_burst.yml
commands.purpose: Lint a Sigma rule and translate it to a Splunk query for review.

facts.title: False positives scale with volume, and precision depends on prevalence
facts.fact: A false-positive rate is only meaningful next to the number of events it is applied to. One percent of one million daily events is ten thousand false alerts, while the same rate on a thousand events is ten. Precision also depends on how rare the true behaviour is: when the base rate is very low, even a sensitive and specific rule produces mostly false positives, so a high alert count is not proof that the rule is badly written.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: Track true positives, false positives and missed cases separately; a single accuracy number hides the trade-off.
Precision is true positives divided by all alerts; recall is true positives divided by all real instances.
Cost asymmetry matters: missing a domain-controller compromise may be far worse than investigating extra alerts.
Prevalence changes over time and across environments, so re-measure rather than reusing a vendor claim.
pitfalls: Quoting a percentage false-positive rate without the event volume it applies to.
Comparing rules by alert count instead of by precision and recall on a labelled sample.

mcqs.question: A rule has a 1% false-positive rate and evaluates 1,000,000 events per day. How many false positives per day does that imply?
mcqs.rationale: One percent of one million is ten thousand. This is why a rate that sounds small can still overwhelm a queue, and why volume must be part of the evaluation.

misconceptions.claim: A detector that is 99% accurate is reliable regardless of how rare the behaviour is.
misconceptions.correction: Accuracy mixes both error types and ignores prevalence. When the true behaviour is extremely rare, most positive alerts can still be false, so precision must be computed from the actual base rate in the environment.

facts.title: Detections fail silently when data quality changes
facts.fact: A rule is only as good as the fields it reads. Parser upgrades, schema migrations, timezone changes, sampling, message truncation and ingestion lag can remove or rename a field without producing an error. The rule continues to run and simply stops matching, which looks like the behaviour disappeared. Pipeline health, field-presence checks and canary events should be monitored alongside rule results.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: A canary event with known content can prove end-to-end parsing after every deployment.
Field-presence dashboards catch a source that is still sending but no longer populating a key field.
Ingestion lag makes a rule evaluate incomplete windows and miss late data.
Sampling at the collection layer can drop the exact events a rare detection needs.
pitfalls: Assuming no alerts means no activity rather than a broken parser.
Validating a rule on raw fixtures while production goes through a different normalization path.

logs.context: Pipeline parse failure caused by a null source address
logs.text: {"time":"2026-11-18T08:14:22.631Z","level":"warn","pipeline":"linux-auth","message":"failed to parse field source.ip: value '-' is not an IP address","event.original":"Failed password for jdoe from  port 51001 ssh2"}
logs.reading: The source address is missing in the original line, so the parser cannot populate source.ip. Any rule that groups by source.ip will drop this event or place it in a null bucket. The warning is the visible symptom; a field-presence check would show the wider gap.

mcqs.question: A detection silently stops matching after a log pipeline upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: A field the rule references was renamed or dropped during normalization
The attacker disabled the rule in the SIEM
The rule's ATT&CK mapping expired
The alert queue reached its storage limit
mcqs.rationale: Pipeline changes can rename fields, change types or stop populating them, and the rule then matches nothing without erroring. Canary events and field-presence monitoring surface this class of failure.

facts.title: The lifecycle of a detection rule
facts.fact: A rule moves through proposal, prototyping, testing, deployment, tuning, review and retirement. Each stage needs an owner, a data-source assumption and a success criterion. Rules should be reviewed on a schedule and when the underlying log source, attacker behaviour or business asset changes. Retirement is a normal outcome, not a failure, and a stale rule that no longer matches anything is worse than no rule because it implies coverage that does not exist.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: Proposal should state the behaviour, the data source and the expected false positives before any query is written.
Deployment should record the rule version and the date it went live.
Review should check whether the rule still fires, whether its suppressions are still valid and whether the owner still exists.
pitfalls: Leaving orphaned rules after the owning team changes.
Keeping a rule because it once caught something, even though its data source is gone.

logs.context: Detection deployment record from a CI pipeline
logs.text: 2026-11-18T10:00:00Z detection-ci[42]: rule=ssh_auth_failure_burst version=3 action=deploy backend=splunk result=success owner=soc-eng
logs.reading: The deployment record ties a rule version to a backend, an owner and a result. A failed translation would show result=failure and should block the release; without this record, a rule present in the repository but missing from the SIEM would look deployed.

mcqs.question: When should a detection rule be retired?
options: When its data source no longer exists or it can no longer be tuned to an acceptable rate
Only when the SIEM licence expires
When it has been deployed for exactly one year
When a newer rule uses a different name
mcqs.rationale: Retirement is driven by loss of data, loss of relevance or an unmanageable error rate with no viable tuning path. Age alone is not a reason, and duplicate rules should be consolidated rather than left to drift.

facts.title: A hunting hypothesis must be falsifiable
facts.fact: A threat hunt starts with a specific, testable statement about adversary behaviour in this environment, not with a generic instruction to look for badness. A usable hypothesis names the actor or technique, the expected observable, the data source that would contain it and the time range. It also states what evidence would disprove it, so the hunt can end with a clear answer rather than an open-ended search.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Derive hypotheses from ATT&CK gaps, threat intelligence relevant to the sector, or anomalies left by past incidents.
Write the expected query result before running the query, to avoid rationalising whatever appears.
Record negative results; they are coverage evidence and can justify new collection.
pitfalls: Starting with a tool rather than a question, then searching for a use for the tool.
Treating a hunt as a dashboard review with no stated hypothesis.

mcqs.question: Which is a well-formed threat-hunting hypothesis?
options: If an intruder used valid accounts, we will see a service account authenticating to servers it has never accessed before
Attackers may be in the network
We should check the SIEM for suspicious activity
The EDR console looks quiet
mcqs.rationale: The first option names a behaviour, an observable, an implied data source and a comparison baseline, so it can be tested and disproved. The others are unfalsifiable or describe a tool state rather than adversary behaviour.

facts.title: Collecting hunt evidence without destroying it
facts.fact: Hunt evidence must be collected in a way that preserves its value: record the exact query, time range, data source and collection time; export results with hashes; keep original timestamps and field values; and maintain a chain of custody for anything that may become case evidence. Prefer read-only access and remote collection, and avoid running untrusted tools on a host that may be compromised.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

details: Volatile data such as memory, running processes and network connections disappears on reboot, so capture it first when compromise is suspected.
A hash of an export proves integrity only if the hash and the export are stored separately.
Record the clock source and any known skew, because it affects how the evidence timeline is interpreted.
Keep analyst notes with the evidence, including what was not collected and why.
pitfalls: Rebooting a suspect host before capturing memory.
Exporting a query result without saving the query, so the result cannot be reproduced.

logs.context: Evidence collection record for one artifact
logs.text: {"case":"CASE-2026-0412","host":"ws-014.example.internal","artifact":"C:\\Windows\\System32\\winevt\\Logs\\Security.evtx","collected_at":"2026-11-18T10:02:11Z","collector":"analyst-3","method":"remote read-only copy","sha256":"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"}
logs.reading: The record names the case, host, exact artifact path, UTC collection time, collector and method, and stores a SHA-256 digest. That combination lets another analyst verify the copy and reproduce how it was obtained. The hash is synthetic here but would be real in a case.

mcqs.question: Which evidence is most volatile and should be captured first on a suspected compromised host?
options: Memory and active network connections
Files on the disk
Installed application versions
The operating system release
mcqs.rationale: Memory contents and live connections disappear on reboot or shutdown. Disk files and installed software persist and can be collected afterwards, so volatile state has priority when compromise is suspected.

facts.title: Turning a successful hunt into a durable detection
facts.fact: When a hunt finds behaviour worth watching for, the query should become a detection with an owner, a logsource declaration, positive and negative tests, a tuning plan and a review date. The hunt's exploratory query is rarely production-ready: it may be too broad, too slow, or dependent on fields that are not guaranteed. The conversion should preserve the logic while making the assumptions explicit.
details: Translate the hunt into the detection format used by the team, such as Sigma, rather than leaving it as a one-off query.
Add the false positives discovered during the hunt to the rule's documentation.
If the hunt found nothing, record the coverage gap instead of inventing a rule with no evidence.
pitfalls: Deploying the hunt query unchanged and flooding the queue.
Losing the context of why the rule exists once the hunt ticket is closed.

mcqs.question: What should happen when a threat hunt finds no evidence of the hypothesised behaviour?
options: Document the negative result and any coverage gap it reveals
Delete the hunt record to avoid confusion
Deploy a detection anyway to show activity
Conclude that the environment is definitely clean
mcqs.rationale: A negative result is still evidence: it may show that the behaviour is absent, that the data source is missing, or that the hypothesis was poorly specified. Recording it preserves that distinction and supports coverage decisions.

facts.title: Hunts should be designed to disprove, not to confirm
facts.fact: Confirmation bias is the main analytical risk in hunting. An analyst who expects to find lateral movement will interpret ordinary SMB traffic as evidence of it. Strong hunts state competing explanations, define what would falsify the hypothesis, and use baselines and control groups. Negative results and alternative explanations should be documented with the same care as findings.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

details: Ask what else would produce the same observable, such as backup software, a scanner or an administrative script.
Use a control population: compare the suspect host or account with peers that perform similar roles.
Have another analyst review the evidence before a hunt is promoted to an incident.
Measure the hunt programme by hypotheses tested and detections improved, not only by incidents found.
pitfalls: Selecting only the events that support the hypothesis and ignoring the rest of the timeline.
Treating a lack of findings as proof of good security rather than as a statement about the data.

mcqs.question: Which practice most reduces confirmation bias during a hunt?
options: Define competing explanations and a control group before searching
Search only for the indicator you expect to find
Ask the asset owner to confirm the host is compromised
Extend the time range until something unusual appears
mcqs.rationale: Stating alternatives and comparing against similar hosts makes it harder to interpret ordinary activity as confirmation. Searching only for the expected indicator and widening the window until something appears both increase the chance of a false conclusion.

misconceptions.claim: A hunt that finds nothing was wasted effort.
misconceptions.correction: A well-designed negative hunt tests a specific hypothesis and can reveal missing telemetry, weak baselines or a hypothesis that needs refinement. That is coverage evidence, and it is often more useful than a vague finding that cannot be actioned.
